title: Valid, Sound, and Precise
text:
Scholars of rhetoric often distinguish between an argument that is valid and one that is sound. An argument is valid when its conclusion follows logically from its premises, even if those premises are false. It is sound only when it is valid and every premise is actually true. Consequently, a speaker may construct a flawless syllogism that nonetheless persuades no one, because its premises are doubtful.

Precision in vocabulary matters because loosely chosen terms can quietly shift a debate. Words such as 'freedom' or 'fairness' carry connotations that differ across audiences, and a writer who fails to define them invites equivocation. A more disciplined arguer therefore states definitions at the outset and holds them constant. Such discipline does not guarantee agreement, yet it makes disagreement far more productive.

questions.text: According to the passage, when is an argument described as sound?
options: When its conclusion follows logically from its premises, even if the premises are false
When it is valid and every premise is actually true
When it persuades most of the listeners
When all of its premises are doubtful

questions.text: According to the passage, what does a disciplined arguer do at the outset of a debate?
options: States definitions and holds them constant
Avoids using words such as 'freedom' or 'fairness'
Asks the audience to define the key terms

questions.text: What can be inferred about a valid argument whose premises are doubtful?
options: It is always persuasive to every audience
It may still fail to convince, because it is not sound
It cannot be constructed according to logical rules

questions.text: What does the author imply about the relationship between precise vocabulary and agreement?
options: Precise vocabulary guarantees agreement among debaters
Precise vocabulary does not ensure agreement, but it can make disagreement more productive
Precise vocabulary is unnecessary in an ordinary debate
Precise vocabulary matters only in legal writing

vocabulary.definition: an argument whose conclusion logically follows from its premises
an argument that is valid and has only true premises
the use of one word with two different meanings in the same argument, to mislead
the additional ideas or feelings that a word suggests beyond its literal meaning

paragraph_translations: Дослідники риторики часто розрізняють аргумент, який є логічно коректним, і аргумент, який є обґрунтованим. Аргумент є логічно коректним, коли його висновок логічно випливає з посилок, навіть якщо ці посилки хибні. Він є обґрунтованим лише тоді, коли він коректний і кожна посилка насправді істинна. Отже, промовець може побудувати бездоганний силогізм, який, проте, нікого не переконає, бо його посилки викликають сумнів.

Точність у словнику важлива, адже недбало обрані терміни можуть непомітно змінити хід дискусії. Слова на кшталт «свобода» чи «справедливість» мають конотації, які різняться для різних аудиторій, і автор, який не визначає їх, допускає логічну підміну значень. Тому більш дисциплінований мислитель формулює визначення на початку й тримається їх незмінно. Така дисципліна не гарантує згоди, проте робить незгоду набагато продуктивнішою.
